The published surrogate, configurationSha256, binds only classpath *paths*, so a dependency republished at the same coordinates leaves every published suite column unchanged.

The aggregate's completeness claim is stated over registered hardening projects only, but neither the manifest nor the console line records how many Gradle-root projects were *not* registered, so the claim is not self-auditing.

The per-project 'up to N concurrently' line is printed once per project, which reads as a per-project bound and contradicts the reader's expectation set by HARDENING.md ('bounds concurrent fuzz children across all selected projects'). The behaviour is correct; only the wording is ambiguous.

The root aggregate fails the build if it cannot delete its own sentinel, but the project certification and the fuzz campaign silently ignore the same failure — producing BUILD SUCCESSFUL alongside receipt-plus-sentinel, which HARDENING.md tells consumers to reject as an incomplete attempt, with no diagnostic explaining why.

On the interrupt branch the barrier re-sets the thread's interrupt flag before throwing, and the publisher's recovery block then performs file I/O on that still-interrupted thread. If that I/O uses interruptible NIO channels it throws ClosedByInterruptException, gets swallowed as a suppressed exception, and the `refused\t<reason>` marker HARDENING.md promises is never written.

f8ba7a3 narrowed the aggregate session from per-Gradle-root state to a single global barrier: the registry's duplicate guard is keyed by root, but the barrier's is global and its state is never cleared, so a second root in one build service instance dies on an internal-sounding check instead of a scoped refusal.

The f8ba7a3 completion barrier emits no output at any log level, so the certification log cannot show whether it engaged. The answer to question (c) is therefore 'no sign of the old race, and no positive evidence either' — the fix is unobservable from the release evidence.

Evidence-bundle defect, not a plugin defect: each SHA256SUMS.txt lists itself with the empty-file digest, so verifying the bundle with the obvious command reports a failure on an otherwise perfect archive. The certification bundle has no checksum file at all.
The draft names two no-record suites; the receipt has four. The two it names are the two that *changed*, but the sentence reads as an inventory of the current state.

The list of moved columns is incomplete and the stated cause is wrong for the omitted one: configurationSha256 also moved, for all four sava-rpc suites and none of sava-core's thirteen, and the cause is a dependency bump rather than a source change.

Unverifiable from the available evidence, and therefore reported as such: three consecutive invocations report that settings.gradle.kts changed when it demonstrably did not. I cannot attribute this to sava-build without a controlled repro, which the read-only constraint forbids.

The certification receipt records nothing about the ordinary-test outcome, so a reader of the receipt alone cannot tell whether `test` executed in the certifying invocation or was carried in UP-TO-DATE from an earlier one — which is exactly what happened here.

Removing the deprecated `sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)` will not break callers — it will silently rebind `tx.sign(list)` to the by-key `sign(Collection<Signer>)`, flipping positional signing to key-matched signing with no compile error.
scenario: Consumer code today: `List<Signer> signers = List.of(feePayer, authority); tx.sign(signers);` binds to `sign(SequencedCollection)` (Transaction.java:784) and signs positionally. That method is now `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)`. When it is removed, `sign(Collection<Signer>)` (Transaction.java:773) is still applicable to a `List`, so the exact same source keeps compiling and now validates and signs by public key. A caller who deliberately relied on positional order — for example signing a message whose slot 0 signer is not the first element, which the deprecated overload permitted — either gets signatures in different slots or a new `IllegalArgumentException` at runtime for an assignment that used to succeed. This is the single most-used signing entry point, and it is the only one of the nine deprecated members with a silently-absorbing sibling: `sign(byte[], SequencedCollection)`, `sign(String, SequencedCollection)`, all three `signAndBase64Encode(*, SequencedCollection)` forms and the three deprecated statics have no `Collection` counterpart, so those call sites would fail to compile at removal, which is the behaviour `forRemoval` normally advertises.

text: The deprecated `sign(SequencedCollection)` is abstract and is the only implementation hook for positional signing, so third-party implementors are forced to implement a `forRemoval` method and the deprecation cannot be honoured without a second breaking change that MIGRATION.md promises will not happen.
scenario: A third-party class `implements Transaction` must supply `sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)` because it is abstract. There is no non-deprecated method it can implement instead: `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` (Transaction.java:845) is a `default` that calls `sign(signers)`, and all five other `signInOrder*` defaults (lines 850, 855, 860, 865, 870) likewise delegate to deprecated members. So an implementor recompiling against this release gets an unavoidable deprecation warning (JLS 9.6.4.6 makes overriding a use), with no migration available. When the removal actually happens, `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` has nothing left to delegate to and must become abstract — which breaks source and binary compatibility for every third-party `Transaction`, directly contradicting MIGRATION.md:106-107 ("New instance methods have defaults, so existing `Transaction` implementations do not need additional method overrides"). The deprecation as written is therefore not executable as an additive change, which is exactly what AGENTS.md's published-library rule is meant to prevent.

text: The deprecation stops at sava-core: `SolanaRpcClient.sendTransaction(..., SequencedCollection<Signer>, byte[])` still funnels through the deprecated positional overload and has no by-key counterpart, so a consumer who follows MIGRATION.md cannot reach `signByKey` through the RPC client.
scenario: A consumer reads MIGRATION.md:93 ("tx.signByKey(signers); // Matches required signer keys, regardless of list order") and wants that behaviour for a multi-signer submission. The only multi-signer send path is `SolanaRpcClient.sendTransaction(Transaction, SequencedCollection<Signer>, byte[])` (SolanaRpcClient.java:930), whose implementation at SolanaJsonRpcClient.java:1591 calls `transaction.signAndBase64Encode(recentBlockHash, signers)` — the method deprecated at Transaction.java:817-822. The consumer therefore gets positional signing regardless, and the only escape is to sign manually and call `sendTransaction(String base64SignedTx)`. Separately, `SolanaJsonRpcClient.java:1591` and `BaseTransaction.java:189` are the library's own unmigrated call sites of methods this commit marked `forRemoval`, so sava-rpc will stop compiling at removal.

text: Bundling the byte-array-ownership decision into a `feat(tx)` commit means the release notes will show one line about signing and will surface neither the nine `forRemoval` deprecations nor the resolution of the documented `Object.hashCode()` contract defect.
scenario: release-please-config.json sets `"release-type": "simple"`, and every entry in CHANGELOG.md is subject-only — commit bodies appear only under `### BREAKING CHANGES`, sourced from `BREAKING CHANGE:` footers (see the 25.10.0 and 25.9.1 sections). This commit has no such footer, so the next release renders exactly `* **tx:** add explicit signing APIs (1dded1d)` under `### Features`. The body sentence "Deprecate positional signing overloads ... and document byte-array ownership" is dropped entirely. Concretely: a consumer scanning the release notes for `forRemoval` deprecations before upgrading finds nothing and never learns MIGRATION.md gained a new section; and a maintainer later auditing "was the PublicKey hashCode-contract issue ever decided?" greps the changelog and finds no trace, because the answer was made under a `tx` scope. The old javadoc explicitly deferred this — "This is retained pending an owner decision" — and the new text resolves it as a permanent caller obligation, which is an owner decision about a different class in a different package from the commit's subject.

text: `signInOrder` and `signByKey` are not a parallel pair and `signInOrder` does not state the mechanism, so the name conveys an ordering nicety rather than "public keys are ignored" — the exact misunderstanding the rename exists to prevent.
scenario: A developer arriving from the Rust SDK, where `Transaction::sign(keypairs, blockhash)` matches by public key and errors with `SignerError::KeypairPubkeyMismatch`, reads `tx.signInOrder(signers)` as "sign, in the order given" — a statement about the order signatures are produced, which is true of every implementation and carries no warning. They pass a `List<Signer>` built from `map.values()` or a set iteration; every javadoc guard is satisfied (the size matches `numSigners()`), signing succeeds, and the payload is rejected on-chain with a signature-verification failure that has no local reproduction. `signByPosition(signers)` or `signBySlot(signers)` pairs grammatically with `signByKey(signers)` and names the mechanism, so the two are read as alternatives rather than as "the ordered one" versus "the keyed one". Note also that Rust has no by-iteration-order API at all — its positional form is `partial_sign_unchecked(keypairs, positions, blockhash)`, taking explicit positions — so sava's positional semantics has no ecosystem analogue and needs a name that carries the warning, not one that reads as a detail. This is cheap to change now and a breaking rename once published.

text: Five of the six new `signInOrder` instance methods bypass `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` and delegate straight to the deprecated members, so overriding the surviving name yields an internally inconsistent object today and a silent behaviour flip when the deprecated names are removed.
scenario: A consumer follows MIGRATION.md and migrates their `Transaction` implementation to the surviving name:      @Override public void signInOrder(SequencedCollection<Signer> s) { auditLog(s); Transaction.super.signInOrder(s); }  `myTx.signInOrder(signers)` runs the override (:845 -> :846 -> abstract `sign(SequencedCollection)`). `myTx.signInOrder(blockHash, signers)` does NOT: :855 -> :856 calls `sign(recentBlockHash, signers)` at :801, whose body is `setRecentBlockHash(...); sign(signers);` -> the abstract seam. The override never runs and the transaction is signed with no audit record. Same for `signInOrderAndBase64Encode(signers)` (:850 -> :851 -> `signAndBase64Encode(SequencedCollection)` at :791 -> `sign(signers)`), `signInOrder(String, ...)` (:860), and both blockhash Base64 variants (:865, :870). Only 1 of 6 entry points sees the override. The identical move on the by-key side works: overriding `signByKey(Collection)` at :883 IS honoured by :888, :894, :900, :906 and :912, because those funnel through it. Nothing at the declarations says the two families differ, and the one-line javadocs at :854/:859/:864/:869 never name the method they delegate to. Then, when the deprecated members at :791/:801/:811/:822/:833 are removed, those five bodies must be re-pointed at `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` — at which point the consumer's override starts running on all six paths. That is a behaviour change delivered BY the removal, which is exactly what a deprecation cycle exists to avoid.

text: `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)` on an ABSTRACT interface method forces a compiler warning on every implementor that they cannot avoid, and the method cannot actually be removed without a second source-incompatible break of `Transaction`.
scenario: (a) Warning every implementor must eat. `void sign(SequencedCollection<Signer> signers)` is abstract, so a third-party `Transaction` MUST declare it. javac enables `[removal]` by default (unlike `deprecation`) and fires it on an override, not just a call. I confirmed this with javac 25.0.2 on a minimal repro and on this repo: compiling sava-core's main source set at 1dded1d^ gives 0 warnings; at 1dded1d it gives   BaseTransaction.java:183: warning: [removal] sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>) in Transaction has been deprecated and marked for removal   BaseTransaction.java:189: warning: [removal] sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>,byte[],int,int,int) in Transaction has been deprecated and marked for removal A consumer whose build uses `-Werror` (or Gradle `options.compilerArgs.add("-Werror")`, common in library projects) stops compiling on upgrade at their own `@Override public void sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)`. Their only escapes are annotating their override `@Deprecated` — which propagates the warning to all of their callers — or `@SuppressWarnings("removal")`. This commit added neither annotation anywhere: not on BaseTransaction.java:183, not on PreV1InterfaceShapeTests.java:70, not on SigningCountTests.java:540. (b) The removal is not reachable additively. `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` at :845 holds no implementation — the implementation lives in each implementor's override of the method being removed. Delete :784 and :845's body has nothing to call, so `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` must become abstract. Adding an abstract method to `Transaction` is precisely the break `PreV1InterfaceShapeTests` exists to prevent (its class javadoc: "Everything v1 added to those interfaces must therefore arrive as a `default`... adding an abstract method without one stops this file compiling, which is the published-library rule enforced by the compiler"). So the `forRemoval = true` at :784 schedules a break the repo's own compatibility pin forbids.

text: The repo's own published main sources still call the removal-scheduled APIs even where this commit added a drop-in replacement, so sava-core and sava-rpc ship code that will stop compiling at removal.
scenario: BaseTransaction.java:189 calls `Transaction.sign(signers, this.data, messageOffset(), messageLength(), signatureOffset(0))` — the static deprecated at Transaction.java:648-649. The replacement `Transaction.signInOrder(SequencedCollection, byte[], int, int, int)` added by this same commit at Transaction.java:701 is a pure alias (`sign(signers, out, msgOffset, msgLen, sigOffset)`), so this is a zero-risk one-word substitution that was missed; it produces a `[removal]` warning today (verified) and a compile error at removal. sava-rpc/src/main/java/software/sava/rpc/json/http/client/SolanaJsonRpcClient.java:1591 calls `transaction.signAndBase64Encode(recentBlockHash, signers)` with `signers` typed `SequencedCollection<Signer>`, binding to the method deprecated at Transaction.java:822. The replacement `signInOrderAndBase64Encode(byte[], SequencedCollection)` exists at Transaction.java:865. At removal, sava-rpc does not compile. Worse, the RPC surface it implements — `SolanaRpcClient.sendTransaction(Transaction, SequencedCollection<Signer>, byte[])` at SolanaRpcClient.java:930 and the Commitment variant at :934 — is itself a positional-signing API. It was neither deprecated nor given a by-key sibling, so a caller who passes a `List` at the RPC layer still silently gets positional signing with no named alternative and no MIGRATION.md entry — the exact trap this commit set out to close one layer down. Concrete failure today: a consumer building sava-core or sava-rpc from source with `-Xlint:removal -Werror` fails on a clean checkout of HEAD; the same checkout at 1dded1d^ compiles warning-free.

text: MIGRATION.md tells implementors the deprecation costs them nothing, but the deprecated `sign(SequencedCollection)` is abstract, so every implementation is warned now and must be renamed at removal.
scenario: MIGRATION.md:105-107 reads "The existing single-signer, explicit-index, and `Collection<Signer>` overloads remain undeprecated. Named positional aliases delegate to the corresponding existing overload, including custom convenience overrides. New instance methods have defaults, so existing `Transaction` implementations do not need additional method overrides." A maintainer of a third-party `Transaction` reads this, concludes the release is a no-op for them, and upgrades. Their build then emits (or, under `-Werror`, fails on) `[removal] sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>) in Transaction has been deprecated and marked for removal` at their own `@Override` — not at any call site they can change. Nothing in the section states that the deprecated `SequencedCollection` overload at Transaction.java:784 is abstract, that implementing it is itself a flagged use, or that at removal they must rename the override to `signInOrder`. The sentence is literally about the NEW methods and is true of them, which is what makes it misleading: the whole implementor-side cost of the change is the one thing the section does not mention. AGENTS.md:69 requires the deprecation to say "what changed and how to keep the old behaviour"; for an implementor (as opposed to a caller) no such path is stated anywhere.

text: `signInOrder(String, SequencedCollection)` bypasses an override of `sign(byte[], SequencedCollection)` while `signInOrder(byte[], SequencedCollection)` honours it, and the new test overrides both so it cannot detect the split.
scenario: An implementor overrides the single natural seam `sign(byte[] recentBlockHash, SequencedCollection<Signer> signers)` — say to reject an all-zero or expired blockhash before signing — reasonably expecting the `String` overload to Base58-decode and delegate, which is exactly what the single-signer twin does (`sign(String, Signer)` at Transaction.java:755-757 is `sign(Base58.decode(recentBlockHash), signer);`). `tx.signInOrder(hashBytes, signers)` -> :855 -> `sign(byte[], SequencedCollection)` -> the override runs, stale blockhash rejected. `tx.signInOrder(Base58.encode(hashBytes), signers)` -> :860 -> `sign(String, SequencedCollection)` at :811, whose body is `setRecentBlockHash(recentBlockHash); sign(signers);` — it never touches the byte[] overload. The check is skipped and the transaction is signed against the blockhash the implementor meant to reject. Same divergence for `signInOrderAndBase64Encode` at :865 vs :870. The two javadocs (:854 "Sets the recent blockhash before signing every required slot in iteration order." and :859 "Sets the Base58 recent blockhash before signing every required slot in iteration order.") assert equivalence and say nothing about the different seam. The by-key family has no such split: :894 and :900 both funnel to `signByKey(Collection)`. The new test `positionalConvenienceAliasesPreserveExistingOverridesAndArguments` overrides BOTH `sign(byte[], SequencedCollection)` (PreV1InterfaceShapeTests.java:441) and `sign(String, SequencedCollection)` (:448), so it passes either way and cannot catch the divergence.

text: The new javadoc scopes the `data()`-returns-a-copy guarantee to "these factories" (the ranged ones), implying the `createDiscriminator(byte[])` it documents does not copy, but `DiscriminatorRecord.data()` copies unconditionally for every factory.
scenario: A caller reads the javadoc on `createDiscriminator(byte[])`, which says the array is "retain[ed] ... without copying" and then that `data()` "returns a copy for discriminators created by these factories" — the nearest and only antecedent being "The ranged factories" in the same sentence. Concluding that `data()` aliases the retained array for this factory, they write:      final byte[] raw = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8};     final var d = Discriminator.createDiscriminator(raw);     final byte[] view = d.data();   // believed to alias d's storage     view[0] = 0x7f;                 // expected to update d     d.equals(view, 0);              // returns FALSE — d still holds 1  The mutation is silently discarded because `DiscriminatorRecord.data()` returns `Arrays.copyOf(...)`. The opposite misreading is just as costly: a hot-path caller who believes only ranged-factory discriminators are safe to hand out adds a defensive `d.data().clone()`, doubling an allocation that was already defensive.

text: The rewrite converts the retained-array/stale-cache defect from "pending an owner decision" into a documented caller obligation, but the test that pins the behaviour still documents it as an unresolved contradiction and explicitly forbids presenting it as intended semantics, so the two now state opposite intent.
scenario: A maintainer auditing whether the hashCode-contract violation is still open reads PublicKeyTest.java:46-48 and the method name and concludes the owner has not decided, so the behaviour may still be changed to a defensive copy; a consumer reads PublicKey.java:170 and concludes the retention is a settled contract they may rely on. Exactly one of these is true after this commit, and nothing in the commit says which. Concretely, the next person who acts on the test's standing instruction ("do not present it as intended value semantics") would revert the javadoc this commit just wrote.

text: The only concrete example given for "sharing depends on the implementation" — "a lookup-table view copies its key slice" — names the one PublicKey implementation the library never constructs, while the lookup-table key type it does hand out shares its array from toByteArray().
scenario: A consumer holding an `AccountIndexLookupTableEntry` — which the SDK produces at TableAccountMeta.java:47 and hands to callers through the public `Instruction.serialize(byte[], int, AccountIndexLookupTableEntry[])` (Instruction.java:57) and `LookupTableAccountMeta.indexWrites/indexReads` (LookupTableAccountMeta.java:52-54) — reads CONVENTIONS.md:72-73, sees that lookup-table keys copy their slice, and treats `entry.toByteArray()` as a private copy: `final byte[] k = entry.toByteArray(); k[0] ^= 1;`. That writes straight through to the entry's retained `publicKey` array (AccountIndexLookupTableEntry.java:51-53 returns the field itself), silently corrupting the key used by `lookupAccountIndex`/`indexOfOrThrow` and therefore the account index written into the serialized transaction.

text: The migration section tells consumers to "use the explicit names to choose the behavior", but the SDK's own undeprecated RPC send path hard-wires the deprecated positional overload and has no named replacement, which the section never says.
scenario: A consumer whose only signing call is `rpcClient.sendTransaction(tx, List.of(feePayer, authority), blockHash)` follows this section, greps their code for `sign`/`signAndBase64Encode`, finds nothing to change, and concludes they are migrated. They are not: `SolanaJsonRpcClient.java:1591` calls `transaction.signAndBase64Encode(recentBlockHash, signers)`, which this commit marked `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)` at Transaction.java:821-822. Because the RPC interface method itself carries no `@Deprecated`, javac emits no warning at their call site, and they will be broken at removal with zero prior signal. They also cannot get by-key behaviour through the RPC client at all — `SolanaRpcClient` declares only `SequencedCollection<Signer>` — so the section's central instruction is unactionable for them.

text: New instance methods have defaults, so existing Transaction implementations do not need additional method overrides is true only of the new methods, and the section never tells implementors that the one abstract member in the deprecated set is itself marked for removal.
scenario: A third-party `Transaction` implementor reads this section, sees the closing sentence, and concludes there is nothing for them to do. But `void sign(SequencedCollection<Signer> signers)` at Transaction.java:783-784 is abstract AND `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)` — the only abstract member in the deprecated set — so they must keep implementing a for-removal method, and javac issues no deprecation warning for merely overriding one, so they get no signal. At removal, `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` (Transaction.java:845-847), which today is a default that delegates to that abstract method, has to become abstract itself — requiring from that implementor exactly the "additional method override" this sentence says is unnecessary. The audience with actual work to do is the one the section reassures.

text: Removing the deprecated positional `sign(SequencedCollection)` will silently rebind every existing `tx.sign(someList)` call site to the by-key `sign(Collection)`, changing which signer fills which slot with no compile error and no warning in MIGRATION.md.
scenario: A consumer today writes `List<Signer> signers = List.of(authority, feePayer); tx.sign(signers);`. Java binds that to `sign(SequencedCollection)` (Transaction.java:784) and signs positionally: `authority` fills slot 0, `feePayer` fills slot 1 — the exact behaviour the new test `aListSelectsPositionalOrByKeySigningByName` pins for `signInOrder(reversed)`. Once that overload is removed (it is `forRemoval = true`), the identical source still compiles, because `List` is a `Collection`, and now binds to `sign(Collection)` (Transaction.java:773), which signs by public key: `feePayer` fills slot 0, `authority` fills slot 1. The transaction still serializes, still has 64 non-zero bytes in every slot, and `getBase58Id()` still returns a signature — it is simply a different, silently re-assigned transaction id. Contrast `signAndBase64Encode(list)`, `sign(hash, list)` and `sign(base58Hash, list)`, which fail loudly at removal because no `Collection` sibling exists; `sign(list)` is the one call shape that rebinds instead of breaking.

text: Five of the six new `signInOrder*` instance defaults route through the deprecated `sign*` chain instead of through `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)`, so an override of the new positional name is honoured by only one of its six entry points — the opposite of the `signByKey` family, where all six funnel through `signByKey(Collection)`.
scenario: A consumer implementing `Transaction` migrates off the `forRemoval` name by overriding the new one: `@Override public void signInOrder(SequencedCollection<Signer> signers) { audit(signers); super.signInOrder(signers); }`. `tx.signInOrder(signers)` runs the audit. `tx.signInOrder(blockHash, signers)` does not — it calls `sign(recentBlockHash, signers)` (Transaction.java:856), which calls `setRecentBlockHash` then the abstract `sign(signers)`, never touching the override. Same for `signInOrder(base58Hash, signers)`, `signInOrderAndBase64Encode(signers)`, and both blockhash Base64 variants: the transaction is signed with the audit hook silently skipped. The equivalent `signByKey` override is honoured by all six of its entry points (Transaction.java:889, 896, 902, 907, 913 all call `signByKey(...)` virtually). A second consequence: because every `signInOrder*` default body is written purely in terms of members marked `forRemoval`, none of them has a body that survives removal, so MIGRATION.md:106-107's "New instance methods have defaults, so existing `Transaction` implementations do not need additional method overrides" stops being true the moment the deprecated members go.

text: The published RPC client's own sign-and-send path still calls the newly `forRemoval` positional `signAndBase64Encode(byte[], SequencedCollection)`, and its public `SolanaRpcClient.sendTransaction(..., SequencedCollection<Signer>, ...)` facade is left undeprecated and undocumented as positional.
scenario: A consumer calls `rpcClient.sendTransaction(tx, List.of(authority, feePayer), recentBlockHash)`. That reaches `transaction.signAndBase64Encode(recentBlockHash, signers)` at SolanaJsonRpcClient.java:1591, which now resolves to Transaction.java:822 — a method this commit marked `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)`. Two concrete outcomes: (a) sava-rpc's own main source set now compiles against a for-removal API, so the module emits deprecation warnings on every build and will fail to compile at removal; (b) `SolanaRpcClient.java:930-937` declares those `SequencedCollection<Signer>` overloads with no javadoc at all, so the SDK's most-used signing entry point still silently signs positionally while `Transaction`'s own docs, CONVENTIONS.md:57-62 and MIGRATION.md:80-107 all now tell callers that positional signing is the deprecated behaviour to migrate away from. Nothing in the commit gives an RPC caller a by-key send path.

text: `signByKey(byte[]|String, Collection)` writes the new blockhash before validating the assignment, so a rejected by-key call leaves the buffer's existing signatures intact over a *changed* message — which the family's headline promise "Assignment-validation failures leave every signature untouched" reads as the opposite of.
scenario: A caller holds a fully signed transaction (`tx.signByKey(oldHash, List.of(feePayer, authority))` succeeded) and retries with a fresh blockhash but a stale signer list that has drifted: `tx.signByKey(newHash, List.of(feePayer, feePayer))`. `setRecentBlockHash(newHash)` runs first (Transaction.java:895) and rewrites 32 bytes of the message in place; `signByKey(signers)` then throws `IllegalArgumentException: Duplicate signer …` from BaseTransaction.java:208. The caller catches the exception, reads the `signByKey` contract at Transaction.java:877 ("Assignment-validation failures leave every signature untouched"), concludes the transaction is unchanged, and submits the previously signed payload. The signature slots are indeed untouched — but they now sign the *old* blockhash while the buffer carries the new one, so `feePayerSignatureOffset` still reports a signature, `getBase58Id()` still returns 64 non-zero bytes, and the cluster rejects it with a signature-verification failure rather than any locally detectable error. The equivalent `signInOrder(byte[]/String, …)` pair has the same hazard. The commit's own rollback test (`NamedTransactionSigningTests.namedSigningRejectsBadAssignmentsWithoutTouchingExistingSignatures`) only exercises the no-blockhash variants, so nothing pins this.

text: `signInOrderAndBase64Encode(SequencedCollection)` promises it "returns the complete signed payload encoded as Base64", but it is a bare forward to the overridable deprecated `signAndBase64Encode(SequencedCollection)` — and the commit's own test asserts it returning a string that is not Base64 of any payload.
scenario: `PreV1InterfaceShapeTests.positionalConvenienceAliasesPreserveExistingOverridesAndArguments` builds a `Transaction` whose `signAndBase64Encode(SequencedCollection)` override returns the literal `"existing-ordered-encoding"`, then asserts `assertEquals("existing-ordered-encoding", existing.signInOrderAndBase64Encode(expectedSigners))`. So the repository itself demonstrates the documented contract being violated through the sanctioned delegation path. A caller who trusts the javadoc and writes `Base64.getDecoder().decode(tx.signInOrderAndBase64Encode(signers))` gets an `IllegalArgumentException` on any implementation that customised the deprecated convenience — which is exactly the customisation the commit message says it set out to preserve. The same applies to the two blockhash Base64 forwards at :865 and :870. By contrast `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` (:841) and `signByKey(Collection)` (:877) each disclose their delegation in prose, so the omission here is inconsistent within the same commit.

text: The five secondary `signInOrder*` entry points bypass an override of `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)`, while the five secondary `signByKey*` entry points honor an override of `signByKey(Collection)` — opposite, undocumented delegation policies introduced in the same commit.
scenario: A consumer subclass adds policy to the new, non-deprecated name: `class AuditedTx extends ... { @Override public void signInOrder(SequencedCollection<Signer> s) { audit(s); super.signInOrder(s); } }`. `tx.signInOrder(signers)` runs `audit`. `tx.signInOrder(blockHash, signers)` does NOT: line 856 calls `sign(recentBlockHash, signers)` -> `sign(SequencedCollection)`, skipping the override entirely; the transaction is still signed, so the omission is silent. The mirror-image subclass overriding `signByKey(Collection)` sees its override run for all six entry points, because 896/902 call `signByKey(signers)`. I confirmed both outcomes by compiling and running a faithful model: `signInOrder(hash, signers) -> [sign(SequencedCollection)]` versus `signByKey(hash, signers) -> [OVERRIDE signByKey, sign(Collection)]`.

text: `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)` is applied to the abstract `sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)`, which implementors cannot stop implementing; honoring the removal later silently rebinds `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)`'s body from positional to by-key signing rather than failing to compile.
scenario: Two concrete failures. (a) Today: a third-party implementor sees `[removal] sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>) in Transaction has been deprecated and marked for removal`, deletes the override as instructed, and gets `error: MyTx is not abstract and does not override abstract method sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>)`. There is no way to comply — the warning is unactionable, and MIGRATION.md's closing paragraph ("New instance methods have defaults, so existing Transaction implementations do not need additional method overrides") addresses only the additions and never mentions the deprecated abstract method they are forced to keep. (b) At the promised removal: line 846's unchanged body `sign(signers)` still compiles, because `SequencedCollection<Signer>` is a `Collection<Signer>`, and silently retargets to the by-key `sign(Collection)`. I verified this — with the `SequencedCollection` overload deleted, javac emits `invokeinterface sign:(Ljava/util/Collection;)V` with no error and no warning. `signInOrder` would then sign by public key while its javadoc at 838-843 still promises "the first signer writes the first signature slot regardless of its public key". Notably, the sibling bodies at 851/856/861/866/871 would all fail to compile on removal, so this is the one entry point whose breakage is silent.

text: sava-rpc's multi-signer `sendTransaction` still calls the newly `forRemoval` positional `signAndBase64Encode(byte[], SequencedCollection)`, is itself neither deprecated nor documented as positional, and has no by-key sibling — so the migration this commit advertises stops at the module boundary.
scenario: A consumer reads MIGRATION.md:82-92, learns that a `List<Signer>` picks positional signing, and fixes their code by switching `tx.sign(signers)` to `tx.signByKey(signers)`. They then call `rpcClient.sendTransaction(tx, signers, blockHash)` with the same out-of-order `List.of(authority, feePayer)`. That path signs positionally with no deprecation warning and no javadoc hint, the fee payer's signature lands in the authority's slot, and the cluster rejects the submission with a signature-verification failure. There is no `sendTransaction(Transaction, Collection<Signer>, byte[])` to select the behavior they were just told to prefer. Separately, when `signAndBase64Encode(byte[], SequencedCollection)` is actually removed, sava-rpc stops compiling — it is the only production (non-test) caller of a `forRemoval` method left in the repo.

text: The stated rationale for the deprecations is false as applied to the three deprecated static raw-buffer helpers, which have no by-key sibling and therefore cannot exhibit the overload confusion the note describes.
scenario: A consumer of the byte[]-level API reads "A `List<Signer>` selects these overloads even when the caller expects the by-key behavior of `sign(Collection<Signer>)`", checks their own `Transaction.sign(signers, out)` call sites, and looks for the by-key static they were told they might have wanted. There is none: `Transaction` declares no `sign(Collection<Signer>, byte[])`, so `Transaction.sign(list, out)` has exactly one applicable candidate and always did. They are being told a `forRemoval` breaking change on three published statics is justified by an ambiguity that does not exist at that layer. The methods' own `@deprecated` tags give the honest reason (explicit naming), which contradicts the migration note.

text: The brand-new `signByKey`/`signInOrder` methods repeat the invariant `Collection<Signer>` / `SequencedCollection<Signer>` parameterization, so a caller holding a list of their own `Signer` implementation still cannot pass it without copying.
scenario: A consumer with a hardware-wallet signer writes `List<HardwareSigner> signers = ...; tx.signByKey(signers);` and gets `error: incompatible types: List<HardwareSigner> cannot be converted to Collection<Signer>` (javac-verified with the equivalent `List<? extends String>` case). They must allocate a `new ArrayList<Signer>(signers)` purely to satisfy the signature. This is inherited from the pre-commit `sign(Collection<Signer>)` so it is not a regression, but these six `signByKey` and six `signInOrder` methods have no published callers yet, which makes this commit the only cost-free moment to widen them; after release the parameter type is frozen.

text: Eight of the nine new `signInOrder*` methods are implemented by calling the very methods this commit marks `forRemoval`, so the deprecation cannot be honoured by deletion.
scenario: A future maintainer executes the removal the annotations promise and deletes the nine deprecated members. Every `signInOrder*` replacement loses its body simultaneously: the static at line 706 calls the deprecated static `sign(signers, out, msgOffset, msgLen, sigOffset)` (deprecated at 648), line 717 calls deprecated `sign(signers, out)` (663), and the instance defaults at 846, 851, 856, 861, 866 and 871 call the deprecated `sign(SequencedCollection)` (783), `signAndBase64Encode(SequencedCollection)` (790), `sign(byte[],SequencedCollection)` (800), `sign(String,SequencedCollection)` (810) and the two `signAndBase64Encode(hash, ...)` overloads (821, 832). The 846 case is the sharpest: `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` delegates to the deprecated *abstract* `sign(SequencedCollection)`, which is the only hook any implementation provides — removing it leaves the replacement with no implementation to reach and turns a deletion into a re-plumbing of `BaseTransaction` and every third-party implementor. MIGRATION.md's closing claim that 'New instance methods have defaults, so existing `Transaction` implementations do not need additional method overrides' is true only for as long as the deprecated abstract method survives, which the annotation says it will not.

text: namedSigningRejectsBadAssignmentsWithoutTouchingExistingSignatures exercises only the six hash-less rejection paths; the four new hash-taking signByKey* methods mutate the transaction before validating, and the assertion the test is named for would fail on them.
scenario: Extend the existing loop with the obvious next case:    final byte[] otherHash = bytes(Transaction.BLOCK_HASH_LENGTH, 99);   assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> tx.signByKey(otherHash, List.of(feePayer, unknown)));   assertArrayEquals(before, tx.serialized());  The assertArrayEquals FAILS. Transaction.signByKey(byte[], Collection) (Transaction.java:894-897) runs setRecentBlockHash(recentBlockHash) — which System.arraycopy's straight into `data` (BaseTransaction.java:125-130) — before signByKey(signers) reaches the assignment validation in BaseTransaction.sign(Collection) and throws. A caller who does `tx.signByKey(freshBlockhash, wrongSignerSet)` on an already-signed transaction catches the IllegalArgumentException and is left holding a payload whose blockhash is the new one and whose two signatures were computed over the old one: getId() still returns a non-zero id, exceedsSizeLimit() is unchanged, nothing looks wrong, and every signature is invalid on submission. The same hole exists for signByKey(String,Collection) (line 900), signByKeyAndBase64Encode(byte[],Collection) (906) and signByKeyAndBase64Encode(String,Collection) (912). Nothing in the 342 new lines, and nothing in Transaction.java's javadoc, records that the by-key atomicity guarantee ('Assignment-validation failures leave every signature untouched', Transaction.java:876-882) stops applying the moment a blockhash argument is added.

text: The contract that separates signInOrder from signByKey on the accept side — positional signing does not match public keys — is asserted in javadoc three times and pinned by no test in the repository.
scenario: The badAssignment loop pointedly runs List.of(feePayer, feePayer) and List.of(feePayer, unknown) through tx.signByKey only. There is no positive counterpart asserting that tx.signInOrder(List.of(feePayer, unknown)) SUCCEEDS. Every positional test in the commit (aListSelects..., positionalConveniences..., staticNamedSigning..., explicitOffsets...) passes exactly the transaction's own two required signers, merely permuted; TransactionSigningTests does the same (signSequencedCollectionMatchesIndividualSigning:151, sequencedCollectionRemainsPositional:159). Concretely: add a signerIndex(signer) check to BaseTransaction.sign(SequencedCollection) (BaseTransaction.java:183-191), or make Transaction.signInOrder(SequencedCollection) delegate to sign(Collection) when all keys happen to match. All 342 new lines stay green and so does the rest of sava-core — yet a published consumer who positionally signs with a key that is not in the account list (an aggregate/threshold signer, an offline co-signer bound to a slot rather than a key) starts getting IllegalArgumentException, and the deprecation note telling them signInOrder 'retains positional signing' becomes false.

text: positionalConvenienceAliasesPreserveExistingOverridesAndArguments guards the overridable-seam routing for all five positional aliases, but the by-key half has no analogue, so five of the six signByKey* methods can be rewritten to bypass the signByKey(Collection) seam with the suite still green.
scenario: Change Transaction.java:894-897 to `setRecentBlockHash(recentBlockHash); sign(signers);` (and likewise lines 900-903, 906-909, 912-915, 888-891), bypassing the overridable default signByKey(Collection). Every test still passes: the built-in TransactionRecord/V1Transaction reach identical bytes either way, and namedSigningDefaultsReachTheExistingImplementationOverloads only ever calls the one-argument existing.signByKey(reversed) (line 413), never a hash-taking form. A third-party Transaction implementation that overrides the documented by-key entry point signByKey(Collection) — an HSM/remote-signer wrapper, an audit hook — is then silently skipped by signByKeyAndBase64Encode(Collection) and all four hash-taking by-key methods, while its signByKey(reversed) path keeps working, producing an inconsistent surface that only shows up at runtime in a consumer's code.

text: The new '@throws ... or the serialized signature boundary is inconsistent' clause on signInOrder(SequencedCollection, byte[]) is pinned only through the deprecated name it delegates to, which is marked forRemoval.
scenario: namedSigningRejectsBadAssignmentsWithoutTouchingExistingSignatures covers only the count half of the new javadoc's @throws (line 112). The boundary half — V1TransactionSkeleton.requireSignatureBlockOffset(out) rejecting a padded or truncated v1 buffer (Transaction.java:676) — is exercised nowhere through signInOrder; the only coverage is V1SignatureLayoutTests.java:610-632 and StaticSignSignerCountTests, which call the deprecated Transaction.sign(...) directly. Because signInOrder is a pure delegation today the behavior is equivalent, but the moment the deprecated statics are removed under their forRemoval contract, signInOrder must carry its own body and the boundary guarantee it advertises will have no test at all — a padded v1 buffer would sign the wrong span and overwrite the tail of the message with no test failing.

text: The new test's declared independent oracle, 'JDK Ed25519', is the exact implementation under test, so the assertion cannot detect a signing-primitive defect; it is the only test in the class that never cross-checks with the independent BouncyCastle verifier.
scenario: The handoff claim states 'Oracle: API contract and JDK Ed25519' and the in-test comment at line 110 says the expected bytes 'come directly from JDK Ed25519', presenting an oracle independent of the code under test. That statement is false. `KeyPairSigner.createSignature` (sava-core/src/main/java/software/sava/core/accounts/KeyPairSigner.java:63) obtains its signer as `Signature.getInstance(ED25519.getName(), SUN_EC_PROVIDER)`, and the test's expected bytes come from `Signature.getInstance("Ed25519")` with no provider, which resolves to that same SunEC instance — the repo registers no other Ed25519 JCE provider (no `Security.addProvider` call exists anywhere in the tree; BouncyCastle is vendored as plain classes in `software.sava.core.crypto.ed25519.Ed25519Util`, never installed as a provider). Both sides of `assertArrayEquals` are therefore produced by the same deterministic implementation over the same key and message. Concretely: if SunEC's Ed25519 signing were replaced or regressed so that it emitted signatures the cluster rejects, this test still passes, because the reference bytes regress identically. Every neighbouring test in the file avoids this by routing through `assertSignedBy` -> `PublicKey.verifySignature`, which uses the BouncyCastle `Ed25519Signer` path (PublicKey.java:92-100) and is genuinely independent of SunEC. AGENTS.md:113-115 requires 'an oracle independent of the current implementation'.

text: The declaration doc frames the null asymmetry as an intended compatibility guarantee, omits its actual consequence (an undiagnosed NPE when the instruction is built into a transaction), and the surprise was never added to CONVENTIONS.md, the repo's designated index for exactly this family.
scenario: A caller reads `Instruction.extraAccounts`'s new javadoc — 'The built-in implementation ignores a singleton null entry ... but retains null entries in larger lists. This existing size-dependent behavior is preserved for compatibility; callers should supply non-null metas' — and reasonably reads the retained null as inert, especially since CONVENTIONS.md's 'How absence is represented' table teaches that a null entry harmlessly holds its slot for `getAccounts`. It is not inert: `Instruction.createInstruction(program, List.of(a, b), data).extraAccounts(Arrays.asList(null, c))` yields an instruction whose `accounts()` contains null, and passing it to `Transaction.createTx(feePayer, List.of(ix))` throws a bare `NullPointerException` from `TransactionRecord.mergeAccounts` line 101 (`accounts.merge(meta.publicKey(), meta, MERGE_ACCOUNT_META)`) rather than a diagnosed `IllegalArgumentException`. Nothing in the javadoc, the test, or the pitest README says so. Separately, CONVENTIONS.md has no entry for this, although AGENTS.md:65-66 points surprising behaviours at that file and AGENTS.md:517-519 names it as the home for 'API behaviours that are not guessable from a signature: how absence is represented (four different ways)'. Wording it as 'preserved for compatibility' on an *interface* method also reads to third-party `Instruction` implementors as a contract they should replicate, which is stronger than the disproved-equivalence status the pitest README correctly records at README:356-368 ('No declared contract excludes that input').

text: The commit hardens and pins hashCode for unvalidated spans and null components but leaves equals throwing on those same instances — including against itself — with no declaration doc and no test, while MIGRATION.md newly invites callers to use instructions as hash keys.
scenario: `var ix = Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(), new byte[1], 2, 0); ix.equals(ix)` throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Array index out of range: 2` — a reflexivity break in `Object.equals`. text: The new tests certify that `hashCode()` is total for unvalidated spans and null fields — the property that makes such an instruction usable as a hash key — but `equals` still throws for those same objects, and no test or doc covers the round trip.
scenario: `byte[] d = {1}; var a = Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(), d, 0, 2); var b = Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(), d, 0, 2); var set = new HashSet<Instruction>(); set.add(a); set.add(b);` — both take the fallback branch and hash identically (same value-based AccountMeta hash, `List.of()` hash 1, same identity hash for `d`, same offset/len), so HashMap lands them in one bucket, `a != b` fails the reference short-circuit, and `b.equals(a)` reaches `Arrays.equals(d, 0, 2, d, 0, 2)` on a length-1 array -> `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Array index out of range: 2` thrown from inside `HashSet.add`. The same shape with the fixture the test itself blesses at line 323, `Instruction.createInstruction((AccountMeta) null, null, new byte[0], 0, 0)`, throws `NullPointerException` from `programId.equals(ix.programId)` instead — both hash to 0, so they always collide.

text: The corrected `toString` doc stops one case short: for a positive length `Arrays.copyOfRange` zero-pads only when `offset` is within the array; a larger or negative `offset` makes the diagnostic `toString()` throw, and an `offset + len` overflow makes it `OutOfMemoryError`. Neither case is documented or pinned.
scenario: `Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(), new byte[]{1}, 5, 2).toString()` -> `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: arraycopy: length -4 is negative`, so a log statement or debugger inspection kills the caller. `Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(), new byte[]{1}, -1, 1).toString()` -> `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: arraycopy: source index -1 out of bounds for byte[1]`. Worst of the three, `Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(), new byte[]{1}, 1, Integer.MAX_VALUE).toString()` — the exact fixture the new hash test constructs at InstructionBuildingTests.java:316 — wraps `offset + len` to `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, so `copyOfRange` computes `newLength == Integer.MAX_VALUE` and raises `OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit`.

text: This commit newly makes a mutation of the retained backing array strand an instruction inside a `HashSet`/`HashMap`; MIGRATION.md warns about it in prose but no test pins the consequence, contrary to the repo's own precedent for exactly this hazard class.
scenario: `byte[] d = {1,2,3}; var ix = Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(), d, 0, 3); var set = new HashSet<Instruction>(); set.add(ix); d[0] = 9; set.contains(ix);` now returns false and `set.remove(ix)` fails, leaking the entry permanently. Before this commit the hash was `Objects.hashCode(data)` (identity), so mutating `d` left the hash unchanged, the lookup found the right bucket, and the `k == key` reference check in HashMap returned true — `contains` returned true. This is a real behaviour change for any consumer who reuses an instruction data buffer.

text: The new migration section invites consumers to use instructions as HashMap/HashSet keys without saying that `equals` throws for the same unvalidated spans the new `hashCode` was deliberately made total for, and nothing pins that throw.
scenario: `byte[] data = {1, 2}; var a = Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(ACC), data, 0, 4); var b = Instruction.createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(ACC), data, 0, 4);` — both permitted, since `createInstruction` is documented as retaining "the supplied array and span without validation". Both take the fallback branch, which is fully deterministic in programId, accounts, array identity, offset and len, so `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` exactly. `new HashSet<Instruction>()` then `add(a); add(b);` reaches `HashMap.putVal`, whose bucket probe calls `b.equals(a)` on the exact hash match, which calls `Arrays.equals(data, 0, 4, data, 0, 4)` and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Array index out of range: 4`. Same for `map.get(b)` after `map.put(a, v)`, and for `offset = -1` (`Array index out of range: -1`). A consumer following this section's advice therefore gets an unchecked exception out of `HashSet.add`.

text: The rewritten `createInstruction` doc enumerates toString's outcomes for unvalidated spans as "empty" or "zero-padded", but omits that it throws for a positive length with an out-of-range offset.

text: R2's self-referential-oracle defect is closed only for the collection overloads; the two single-`Signer` `sendTransaction` tests still oracle with the exact helper the client calls, and that family has the OPPOSITE (by-key) semantics.
scenario: Change `SolanaJsonRpcClient.java:1575` from `transaction.signAndBase64Encode(recentBlockHash, signer)` to `transaction.signInOrderAndBase64Encode(recentBlockHash, List.of(signer))`. Both `signsWithASingleSignerAndUsesTheDefaultCommitment` and `signsWithASingleSignerAtAnExplicitCommitment` stay green — their `expected` is `transaction(signer).signAndBase64Encode(BLOCK_HASH, signer)`, and because the test's lone signer IS the fee payer, by-key index 0 and positional slot 0 produce identical bytes (both paths also stamp `data[0] = 1`). The whole `check` build stays green. But the observable contract flips: today `rpcClient.sendTransaction(tx, someSignerThatIsNotARequiredAccount, hash)` fails fast client-side with `IllegalArgumentException("Failed to find index for signer ...")` from `BaseTransaction.signerIndex`; after the swap it silently writes that key's signature into slot 0 and submits a transaction the cluster rejects for signature verification. This is exactly the mutation class R2 named, one overload family over, and 25.11.0 is the release that turns signing-order semantics into written API contracts.

text: The single-`Signer` `sendTransaction` overloads sign by public key and throw for a non-required signer, but carry no javadoc, eight lines above siblings that are explicitly documented as positional and key-agnostic.
scenario: A caller reads the contract added at lines 930 and 938 — "signs in iteration order ... without matching its public key to the required account" — and reasonably assumes the adjacent, identically named `sendTransaction(tx, signer, hash)` behaves the same way. It does not: it routes to `Transaction.sign(Signer)`, which resolves the slot by public key and throws `IllegalArgumentException("Failed to find index for signer <key>")` when the signer is not a required account. So `sendTransaction(tx, delegateSigner, hash)` throws while the one-character-different `sendTransaction(tx, List.of(delegateSigner), hash)` succeeds and submits. Nothing at the declaration warns of this, and the commit that made positional signing a written contract left the by-key half of the same method name silent.

text: Named "UsesSignaturePositions", the test only proves keys are not matched; with one required signer it cannot distinguish iteration order, so the "each signer writes the corresponding signature position" half of the documented contract is unverified at the client layer.
scenario: Change `SolanaJsonRpcClient.java:1591` to `transaction.signInOrderAndBase64Encode(recentBlockHash, signers.reversed())` (`SequencedCollection.reversed()` compiles here). Every test in the class stays green, because every RPC test passes exactly one signer and a one-element collection is its own reversal. A real two-signer caller then gets slots 0 and 1 swapped, producing two signatures that both fail verification on-chain — contradicting SolanaRpcClient.java:930/938 verbatim. Core covers ordering thoroughly (`NamedTransactionSigningTests.aListSelectsPositionalOrByKeySigningByName` uses a reversed two-signer list), so the exposure is confined to the client's choice of helper, but that is precisely what this suite exists to pin.

text: CONVENTIONS.md documents the positional/by-key split only at the `Transaction` level, omitting the sharper `SolanaRpcClient.sendTransaction` variant of the same trap, though the file exists so the family is visible in one place.
scenario: A caller consulting CONVENTIONS.md's "Argument-order and flag traps" section learns that `Transaction.sign(List<Signer>)` is positional and `sign(Collection<Signer>)` is by-key, and concludes the trap is confined to `Transaction`. They then write `rpcClient.sendTransaction(tx, signer, hash)` and `rpcClient.sendTransaction(tx, List.of(signer), hash)` interchangeably. The two have different key-matching semantics and different failure modes for a non-required signer (throw vs. submit), and the RPC variant is worse than the documented one because both arms share a single method name and neither arm is deprecated to steer callers to a named alternative. The same section already documents a less severe `sendTransaction` overload trap (`skipPreFlight` selecting a family), so the omission is inconsistent with its own scope.

text: The new javadoc's "renders null or zero-length data as empty" is false for a zero-length or short array with a positive declared length: `toString()` fabricates zero bytes instead, on a path malformed transactions actually reach.
scenario: `Instruction.createInstruction(programId, keys, new byte[0], 0, 4).toString()` renders `"data": "AAAAAA=="` — four zero bytes that do not exist — not the documented empty string. Same for a short array: `createInstruction(programId, keys, new byte[]{1,2}, 1, 5).toString()` renders `"data": "AgAAAA=="`, two real bytes plus three fabricated zeros. Production-reachable: `TransactionSkeleton.deserializeSkeleton` walks instructions at TransactionSkeleton.java:80-95 advancing `o` by each declared compact-u16 `len` with no check against `data.length`, and `if (o < data.length)` at line 95 only selects the lookup-table branch, so a transaction whose LAST instruction declares e.g. 200 data bytes with 3 remaining deserializes without error; `parseInstructions` then builds that instruction at TransactionSkeletonImpl.java:300 and its `toString()` prints 3 real bytes followed by 197 invented zeros. A maintainer diagnosing a truncated transaction from a block or an RPC payload sees plausible base64 instead of evidence of truncation.

text: The commit documents and pins an unvalidated null-data construction that nothing in the repo relies on, instead of adding the additive construction-time check AGENTS.md permits; the deferred failure is an NPE mid-way through writing the caller's serialization buffer.
scenario: `Transaction.createTx(feePayer, List.of(Instruction.createInstruction(program, keys, null, 2, 4)))` — `serializedLength()` (InstructionRecord.java:88-92) succeeds and reserves 4 data bytes it cannot supply, the buffer is allocated at the correct size, then `instruction.serialize(out, i, accountIndexLookupTable)` (Transaction.java:233) reaches `System.arraycopy(data, offset, out, i, len)` at InstructionRecord.java:116 and throws NullPointerException *after* the program-id index, the compact-u16 account count, the account indices and the data-length prefix have already been written into `out`. The same instruction also NPEs from `copyData()` (line 164), `discriminator(n)` (line 141), `wrapDiscriminator(n)` (line 148), `beginsWith(...)` (line 155) and `equals` (line 174) — it cannot even be compared to itself.

text: `InstructionRecord` overrides `equals` value-wise but leaves the record's implicit identity-array `hashCode`, so instructions the repo's own test asserts are equal hash differently.
scenario: Using the exact fixtures from InstructionBuildingTests.equalsComparesDataContentNotBacking (lines 244-249): `plain = createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(ACCOUNT_A), new byte[]{1,2,3,4})` and `sliced = createInstruction(PROGRAM, List.of(ACCOUNT_A), new byte[]{7,1,2,3,4,7}, 1, 4)` satisfy `plain.equals(sliced)` (asserted at line 249), but `new HashSet<>(List.of(plain)).contains(sliced)` returns false, `Map.of(plain, x).get(sliced)` returns null, and `Stream.of(plain, sliced).distinct().count()` returns 2. Any downstream consumer de-duplicating or indexing instructions — the natural thing to do with an SDK type that advertises content equality — silently keeps duplicates or misses lookups. Related to this dimension: for `(null, 2, 4)` `hashCode` returns normally while `equals` throws NPE, so such an instruction can be put in a HashSet but blows up when a colliding lookup compares it.

text: Two behaviours are now documented only at the declaration and are absent from CONVENTIONS.md, whose stated purpose is to make exactly this family visible in one place — and the sharper instruction byte-array trap is documented nowhere at all.
scenario: A caller reads CONVENTIONS.md's "Byte-array ownership" section, which names `PublicKey.createPubKey` and `Discriminator.createDiscriminator` as the array-retaining factories and adds that "the ranged discriminator factories copy", and concludes instruction data is safe. They then write `Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(skeleton.parseInstructions(accounts)[0].data())` and get the base64 of the ENTIRE serialized transaction, not the instruction data — because `createInstruction(programId, keys, data, offset, len)` retains the array (this commit's own new javadoc) and every parsed instruction is handed the whole transaction buffer (TransactionSkeletonImpl.java:300 and V1TransactionSkeleton.java:361 pass the skeleton's `data` field, which is the full tx per BaseTransactionSkeleton.java:22). `copyData()` or `offset()`+`len()` is required; nothing in the index says so. Separately, `extraAccounts(List)`'s size-dependent null handling — documented at Instruction.java:48-50 by 4e43f00 — is exactly a "how absence is represented" convention and is missing from that section too.

text: The new test does not pin the property its name asserts — it cannot distinguish "did not read the span" from "read the span and found it empty", and both of its inputs sit on the side of the guard where the javadoc happens to be right.
scenario: Replace the guard at InstructionRecord.java:188 with `data != null && len > 0 && offset >= 0 && offset + len <= data.length` — a guard that explicitly DOES read the span and the array length, contradicting the test's name and the javadoc's "without reading the span". Both loop iterations still pass (`null, 2, 4` short-circuits on `data != null`; `new byte[0], 2, 0` short-circuits on `len > 0`), so the suite stays green. Conversely, the one input that would expose the javadoc's false half (`new byte[0], 0, 4`, which renders `"data": "AAAAAA=="` — see finding 1) is not covered, so the documented contract and the test agree only by omission.

text: The two re-derived `Transaction.createTx` acceptances rest on the premise that only the compacted front of `sortedAccounts` is observable, but `createTx` is a public static that compacts a caller-supplied array in place, so both accepted mutants are caller-visible.
scenario: Caller invokes the public `Transaction.createTx(List<Instruction>, int, AccountMeta[] sortedAccounts, LookupTableAccountMeta[])` (Transaction.java:435-438) with `sortedAccounts = {payer, lookupA, lookupB, program}` and two lookup tables. The file lists `PublicKey.createPubKey` retention and `toByteArray()` sharing but says nothing about `createTx` reordering the array they passed, so they reuse the array and hit the header/privilege corruption described in finding 1. CONVENTIONS.md:8-9 states the contract this misses: "Where a convention is surprising it is documented at the declaration too; this file exists so the family is visible in one place."

text: The sibling public overload `createTx(List, int, AccountMeta[], AddressLookupTable)` compacts the caller's array in place exactly as the newly documented overload does, but the delta leaves it with no javadoc at all.
scenario: A consumer builds `sortedAccounts` once and calls `Transaction.createTx(instructions, len, sortedAccounts, lookupTable)` (line 266) for a single table. The loop at lines 298-306 rotates included accounts to the front, so `sortedAccounts` comes back reordered. Reading only the declarations, the consumer sees the warning on the four-table overload (lines 435-438) and nothing on this one, concludes this overload is safe, and reuses the array — for a second `createTx` call, or to resolve `sortedAccounts[i]` by an index computed before the call — and silently gets the wrong account.

text: The new javadoc states one uniform post-condition for "one or more lookup tables", but the tail's meaning differs between the two delegated paths: with one table the tail position IS the loaded-address index, with two or more it is not.
scenario: With two tables, the caller reads "accounts included in the message come first, followed by lookup-loaded accounts ... relative order preserved" and takes `sortedAccounts[numIncluded + k]` to be the k-th loaded address of the message. For the delta's own fixture the array tail is `[lookupA, lookupB]` while the wire indexes are lookupB=2 and lookupA=3, so every such mapping is inverted. The same inference is correct under the one-table delegation, which is what makes it a trap.

text: The test pins only the `numLookupTables >= 2` half of the contract the javadoc states for "one or more lookup tables"; the `numLookupTables == 1` delegation has no test that observes the caller's array.
scenario: Change the single-table overload (Transaction.java:298-306) to partition into a fresh array instead of compacting in place — e.g. while cleaning up the deprecated factories before 25.11.0. The serialized bytes are unchanged, so every existing assertion stays green, yet "Pass a clone to preserve the input array's order" at Transaction.java:437 is now false for one table and a consumer who took the javadoc at its word and cloned is doing dead work while one who relied on in-place compaction to read the resulting order is broken.

text: A newly documented caller-visible array-ownership surprise was added at the declaration but not to CONVENTIONS.md, the file whose stated purpose is to make that family visible in one place.
scenario: A consumer follows the file's own instruction ("Read this before writing assertions against an API you have not used here") and reads the `## Byte-array ownership` section. It tells them which factories retain an input array and that they can pass `bytes.clone()`. It says nothing about a factory that reorders an input array. They call the four-arg `createTx` with a reused `sortedAccounts`, reuse it afterward, and get the wrong account order — the exact behavior the delta just documented and that uses the same `clone()` remedy the section already teaches.

text: Only one of the two public array-taking createTx overloads got the new in-place-mutation javadoc; the AddressLookupTable overload compacts the caller's array identically and is still undocumented — and it is the code path the documented overload's own one-table promise is delegated to.
scenario: A consumer holds its own sorted AccountMeta[] and calls Transaction.createTx(instructions, serializedInstructionLength, sorted, lookupTable) (the AddressLookupTable overload at line 266). Lines 273-320 permute `sorted` in place exactly as the documented overload does — message accounts to the front, lookup accounts to the tail. The caller then reuses `sorted` (for a second transaction, or to map account index -> meta) and gets the permuted array: with input [payer, lookupA, lookupB, program] the array is [payer, program, lookupA, lookupB] on return, so index-based lookups and any second createTx call read the wrong accounts. Nothing at the declaration warns them. The same consumer reading the newly documented 4-arg overload is told 'With one or more lookup tables, compacts sortedAccounts in place' — but the one-table case is delivered by line 447 delegating to this undocumented sibling, so the documented sentence is realized by a method whose own signature carries no such notice.

text: CONVENTIONS.md's array-ownership family was not extended with the newly documented caller-array mutation, so the file's stated guarantee that the family is 'visible in one place' no longer holds for the behaviour this delta just established as a published contract.
scenario: A consumer following the repo's own stated navigation reads CONVENTIONS.md's 'Byte-array ownership' section to learn which sava APIs take ownership of caller-supplied arrays. It tells them createPubKey/createDiscriminator retain their input and that they can pass bytes.clone(). It says nothing about Transaction.createTx permuting a caller-supplied AccountMeta[] in place. They conclude no other array-ownership hazard exists, pass their own sorted array to createTx, reuse it, and get the permutation described in the finding above. The file's premise — that it exists so the family is visible in one place — is what makes the omission actively misleading rather than merely incomplete.

text: The 'Result-identical routing' preamble still forward-references an InstructionRecord 'exception' as though a live acceptance exists; the section deletion changed what 'below' points at, and no InstructionRecord row remains in any baseline.
scenario: A maintainer auditing the `# result identical routing` family before 25.11.0 reads line 336-338 — 'two branches retain this equivalence argument after the 2026-09-05 review. The singleton-null exception in InstructionRecord is documented separately below' — and goes looking for the InstructionRecord row that this exception qualifies. There is none: tx-accepted.csv carries zero InstructionRecord rows, and 'below' now lands in '### Retired compatibility acceptances', a record of rows that no longer exist. The sentence reads as pointing at live debt and costs a cross-check every time the family is reviewed; worse, it invites re-adding an acceptance for a mutant that is now killed.

text: The javadoc documents the in-place caller-array mutation on only one of the two public createTx overloads that perform it; the sibling AddressLookupTable overload runs the identical compaction and stays silent, and the documented overload delegates to it.
scenario: A consumer builds `sorted = TransactionRecord.sortV0Accounts(map)` and calls `Transaction.createTx(ixs, len, sorted, table)` (the single-AddressLookupTable overload). Lines 298-306 compact `sorted` in place, so it returns partitioned as {message accounts..., lookup accounts...} and is no longer in VO_META_COMPARATOR order. The consumer, having read no warning on that overload, reuses `sorted` for a second call with a different lookup table that does not carry those accounts. The previously-skipped writable accounts are now included, producing a wire account list ordered payer(write,signer), program(readonly), lookupA(write), lookupB(write) with numReadonlyUnsignedAccounts=1 - so the runtime reads the last non-signer as the readonly one and grants the program account write privilege while stripping it from a writable account.

text: The new zero-table sentence describes that branch as a neutral rebuild, omitting that it silently downgrades the result from versioned/v0 to legacy format and discards the fee-payer designation carried only by sortedAccounts.
scenario: A caller with a v0 pipeline holds `sortedAccounts` containing `AccountMeta.createFeePayer(payer)` for a payer that only pays and appears in no instruction, plus an empty `LookupTableAccountMeta[]` because no ALT applied this time. Line 444 routes to `createTx(instructions)`, which at line 64 passes a null AccountMeta to line 47, so `TransactionRecord.mergeAccounts(null, ...)` (TransactionRecord.java:94-96) never puts the payer into the map. The returned transaction is legacy-format (sortLegacyAccounts + MSG_HEADER_LENGTH at line 206, no VERSIONED_BIT_MASK) and omits the payer entirely: `tx.feePayer()` is null, numRequiredSignatures is one lower than the caller expects, and signature slot 0 belongs to a different account. Nothing in the javadoc predicts either the format change or the dropped payer.

text: CONVENTIONS.md's "Byte-array ownership" section is the repo's stated one-place index for exactly this caller-array-ownership family, and the delta added a new member of it without indexing it there.
scenario: A contributor follows CONVENTIONS.md's own promise at lines 8-9 ("Where a convention is surprising it is documented at the declaration too; this file exists so the family is visible in one place") to learn which sava APIs take ownership of a caller's array. text: The rewritten closing clause of the untriaged-debt paragraph no longer qualifies anything and collides with a different set of entries the same section already calls "historical evidence".

text: F2's EXTENSION_NAMES.length sub-gap is not closed by the new guard, and moving the name lookup onto the error paths made the missing-entry failure latent instead of immediate.
scenario: A maintainer syncs a new upstream extension at wire ID 29: regenerates the fixture to 30 rows, bumps the two hard-coded 29s to 30, adds a record to MintTokenExtension's permits and a 'case 29 -> PermissionedTransferConfig.read(data, i)' arm, but forgets to append a 30th EXTENSION_NAMES entry. Every happy-path parse succeeds (the array is now read only on error paths), the new population guard passes (concreteTypes and fixtureTypes both hold the new class), and the build ships. In production, an on-chain Token-2022 account whose ordinal-29 TLV header declares a length that disagrees with the parsed record makes line 121 evaluate EXTENSION_NAMES[29] and throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 29 out of bounds for length 29 instead of the documented IllegalArgumentException, so any caller catching IllegalArgumentException around parseExtensions/Token2022.read does not catch it.

text: The bijection's 'typed parser dispatch' claim is not established for Uninitialized; fixture row 0 satisfies it through the padding short-circuit, which never reaches the switch.
scenario: Token2022.parseExtensions:57-60 returns Set.of(Uninitialized.INSTANCE) as soon as extensionType == 0, before the dispatch switch, and there is no 'case 0 ->' arm at all. Fixture row 0 is 'ordinal=0 name=Uninitialized len=0 rust_long_accepts=true', so parseTlv(0, value) at line 138 short-circuits, and even the long-value probe parseTlv(0, [0xa5]) returns Uninitialized without reading the declared length (which is why the row is marked accepting). Uninitialized therefore enters fixtureTypes at line 145 with zero dispatch, length-validation, or diagnostic coverage, yet the line-176 message tells the next maintainer that every member of the set has 'typed parser dispatch'. Concretely: broaden the padding short-circuit (say to extensionType <= 1, whether by hand or by a surviving PIT conditionals-boundary mutant) and the bijection still passes for row 0 while wire ID 1 is silently swallowed as padding.

text: The guard's failure output is two unordered ~30-element dumps of fully qualified class names with no diff, so it does not name the type it exists to catch.
scenario: The exact scenario the guard is for -- a maintainer adds one record to the sealed hierarchy and forgets the fixture row -- fails with 'every concrete Token-2022 type needs a pinned Rust fixture and typed parser dispatch ==> expected: <[class software.sava.core.accounts.token.extensions.TokenGroupMember, class software.sava...., ...30 entries in HashSet iteration order...]> but was: <[...29 entries in a different order...]>'. text: The migration guide's headline announces that 25.11.0 introduces transaction format v1 but never states that v1 is not accepted on mainnet, and no consumer-facing javadoc says so either.

With preflight the RPC returns `-32002 Transaction simulation failed: Transaction version is unsupported`; with `skipPreflight` the node returns a signature and the transaction is silently discarded by sigverify, so `getSignatureStatuses` stays null forever and the client hangs waiting for a confirmation that can never arrive. Nothing the consumer read warned them.

scenario: The 25.11.0 handoff record contains no line stating what property the new `assertEquals(concreteTypes, fixtureTypes, ...)` walk pins or what oracle makes it independent of `Token2022.parseExtensions`. A later maintainer who finds this assertion failing after adding a `TokenExtension` subtype has no recorded statement that the fixture — not the Java dispatch — is the authority, and the cheapest way to make it pass is to add the type to the fixture side or to relax the assertion, which is exactly the 'passing assertion that merely locks in the bug' the rule exists to prevent. The owed line is roughly: Property: every concrete permitted subtype of the sealed TokenExtension hierarchy has typed dispatch in parseExtensions and exactly one pinned Rust fixture row, and no two Rust IDs collapse onto one Java type | Oracle: the committed upstream Rust fixture (29 rows) plus `TokenExtension.class.getPermittedSubclasses()`, neither derived from parseExtensions | Outcome: missing assertion added.

text: The three pending-prune rows keep `# line 28` / `# line 37` / `# line 40` tags that point into the `DataEncoding` enum and `DATA_ENCODING_PARSER` lambda `0112d69` added, and the new section never says the tags are historical — the half of F3 that is still open.

text: The 25.11.0 migration guide is shipped with no link from the repository's own documentation entry point; after this commit the string "MIGRATION" appears nowhere in the tree except the .gitignore allow-list.
scenario: A consumer on 25.10.0 upgrades to 25.11.0 and their build fails to compile on `Transaction.MAX_SERIALIZED_LENGTH`.
