text: HEAD ships a knowingly red mutation gate; `:sava-rpc:hardeningCertify` cannot pass, so 25.11.0 cannot be certified, and nothing in CI or the publish path will stop the tag.
scenario: On the committed tree, `./gradlew :sava-rpc:pitestEncodingVerify` fails with "pitest 'encoding': 1 unkilled mutant(s) not in the accepted baseline: software.sava.rpc.json.PrivateKeyEncoding$Parser,createSigner,RemoveConditionalMutator_EQUAL_IF,SURVIVED (newly covered — was NO_COVERAGE; triage, not a refresh)". `hardeningCertify` re-executes every suite, so `:sava-rpc:hardeningCertify` fails at that task and 25.11.0 cannot be certified. Meanwhile `check` is green, build.yml and check-pr.yml both delegate to sava-build's check-only reusable workflows, and publish.yml fires on any `[0-9]*.[0-9]*.[0-9]*` tag push with no hardening step — so pushing tag `25.11.0` publishes sava-core and sava-rpc with the gate still red and no signal anywhere.

text: `Parser.test` marks the deferred `secret` value without skipping it, so any JSON object with `secret` before `encoding` fails to import; this is the bug that makes the mutant unkillable.
scenario: `PrivateKeyEncoding.fromJsonPrivateKey(JsonIterator.parse("{\"secret\":\"<base64 private key>\",\"encoding\":\"base64PrivateKey\"}"))` throws `JsonException` instead of returning a `Signer`. `secretMark = ji.mark()` leaves the cursor at the start of the secret value and returns true, so `testObject` resumes reading a field name from inside the value and dies. All five encodings are affected (the committed test iterates all five and asserts the throw). Because the deferred path can therefore never succeed, `createSigner` is never entered with `signer == null && secretMark != 0`, which is exactly why `RemoveConditionalMutator_EQUAL_IF` on `if (secretMark == 0)` (line 137) survives and why the two `ji.reset(...)` `NakedReceiverMutator` rows stay `NO_COVERAGE`.

text: The regression test that fails against unmodified production exists only under /private/tmp; the repo's committed test is a green assertThrows that locks in the bug.
scenario: /private/tmp is purged on reboot and by macOS periodic cleanup. Once it goes, the README's three cited artifacts (`sava-triage-rpc-field-order-regression.java`, `-tests-red.xml`, `-tests-red.log`) are dangling paths and nothing in the repository reproduces the field-order failure. text: The red `pitestEncoding` gate is absent from HARDENING_NOTES.md, the file AGENTS.md designates for per-suite deviations and the one a release engineer reads before tagging.
scenario: A maintainer preparing 25.11.0 follows AGENTS.md:369-370 ("Per-suite scope decisions, deviations and the full per-package history are in HARDENING_NOTES.md; every accepted mutant's written reason is in the owning module's config/pitest/README.md"). The failing gate is not an accepted mutant's reason, so config/pitest/README.md is the wrong file for it under this repo's own split; the maintainer sees nothing and tags.

text: AGENTS.md assigns `hardeningCertify` to a "local release checklist" that does not exist in the repo, and publish.yml has no hardening gate — the mechanism by which a red gate reaches Maven Central.
scenario: AGENTS.md:98 requires the repo to record whether `hardeningCertify` is owned by CI or by the release checklist; line 381-382 records "the local release checklist, not by CI." No such checklist exists — grep for "release checklist"/"checklist" across every tracked .md and .yml returns only these two AGENTS.md self-references and one 2026-07-21 HARDENING_NOTES heading. `.github/workflows/publish.yml` triggers on `push: tags: ['[0-9]*.[0-9]*.[0-9]*']` and delegates straight to sava-build's publish workflow. So the single named control preventing an uncertified release is a document nobody can open, and tagging `25.11.0` today would publish sava-core and sava-rpc with `pitestEncoding` red without `hardeningCertify` ever running.

text: The failure path this commit chose to document instead of fix throws a JsonException whose message contains the caller's private key in cleartext.
scenario: An operator writes a ravina/kms signing config as {"secret":"BbMQkQYZspmkytduTWvXEtc4mMURjsekJDvty2WtKeSb","encoding":"base58PrivateKey"}. MemorySignerFactory calls fromJsonPrivateKey(ji), which throws systems.comodal.jsoniter.JsonException with getMessage() = `testObject: expected [,{}n], but found: ", offset: 11, context: {"secret":"»BbMQkQYZspmkytduTWvXEtc4mMURjsekJDvty2WtKeSb","encoding":"ba…` — the complete 32-byte seed. Service startup failures of this kind are logged and shipped to log aggregators, so a two-key ordering mistake exfiltrates the signing key.

text: The new javadoc mis-scopes the defect as a field-order rule; the real limitation is that any unrecognized field also aborts the import, so the documented workaround does not save a valid config.
scenario: A user follows the javadoc — "Put `encoding` first to import the object" — and writes {"encoding":"base58PrivateKey","secret":"BbMQ…KeSb","note":"hot wallet"}. encoding precedes secret exactly as instructed, yet fromJsonPrivateKey still throws JsonException: `testObject: expected [,{}n], but found: ", offset: 95, context: …ret":"BbMQkQYZspmkytduTWvXEtc4mMURjsekJDvty2WtKeSb","note":"»hot wallet"}`. The advertised workaround silently does not work, and the user has no way to derive the real rule from the declaration.

text: Retained pending an owner decision leaves the RPC Encoding gate red, which is not one of AGENTS.md's three legal outcomes, and the additive fix that would clear it is already permitted without owner sign-off.
scenario: The 25.11.0 release checklist runs hardeningCertify. The Encoding suite fails on the newly covered PrivateKeyEncoding$Parser.createSigner RemoveConditionalMutator_EQUAL_IF survivor, which this commit deliberately neither killed, refactored, nor accepted with a row label (sava-rpc/config/pitest/README.md:48-49: "That newly covered survivor still fails the gate; it has not been accepted or hidden by a baseline rewrite"). text: A null secret makes the deferred branch reachable and crashes with a NullPointerException, and the enclosing iterator is left mid-object; neither the javadoc's field-order framing nor the new tests cover it.
scenario: fromJsonPrivateKey on {"secret":null,"encoding":"base58PrivateKey"} throws java.lang.NullPointerException: `Cannot invoke "software.sava.rpc.json.PrivateKeyEncoding.ordinal()" because "encoding" is null`. testObject sees the unconsumed `n`, calls skipNull() and returns immediately, so the `encoding` field is never read; createSigner then finds secretMark != 0 and calls fromJsonPrivateKey(ji.reset(secretMark), null), and the enum switch NPEs. Because testObject returned early, an enclosing document (the `[{...},73]` shape the sibling test exercises) is also left with its cursor inside the object.

text: `anUnrecognizedFieldCannotSupplyTheRequiredSecret` passes for a completely different reason than its name states and cannot detect the property it claims to pin.
scenario: The test asserts that {"encoding":"base64PrivateKey","notSecret":"<key>"} throws RuntimeException, implying it verifies that createSigner refuses to accept a non-`secret` field as the secret. In fact execution never reaches createSigner: the unrecognized `notSecret` field's value is left unconsumed by Parser.test, testObject aborts, and the RuntimeException is a JsonException about the JSON grammar. Delete the missing-secret guard at PrivateKeyEncoding.java:137-139 entirely and this test still passes, so it guards nothing it names — and once the parser is fixed to skip unknown fields, it will pass via a third, again different, mechanism (IllegalStateException) without anyone noticing the semantics changed.

text: The new javadoc's documented workaround ("Put `encoding` first to import the object") is not sufficient — any field name other than pubKey/encoding/secret also aborts the import — and the new test that hits this misattributes the cause in its name.
scenario: PrivateKeyEncoding.fromJsonPrivateKey(JsonIterator.parse("{\"encoding\":\"base64PrivateKey\",\"secret\":\"<base64 seed>\",\"note\":\"backup\"}")) follows the documented workaround exactly — encoding precedes secret — and still throws JsonException ("testObject: expected [,{}n], but found: \"") instead of returning the Signer. A consumer reading the new declaration doc will conclude field order is the only limitation and ship a config file with one extra key.

text: A new test pins verbatim an IllegalStateException message that names the field the caller supplied rather than the one that is missing, and the sibling test six lines below feeds it exactly the input where the message is wrong while asserting only the exception type.
scenario: PrivateKeyEncoding.fromJsonPrivateKey(JsonIterator.parse("{\"encoding\":\"base64PrivateKey\"}")) throws IllegalStateException("Must configure 'encoding' field [jsonKeyPairArray, base64PrivateKey, base64KeyPair, base58PrivateKey, base58KeyPair]"). The caller did configure encoding; `secret` is the missing field, and the message never mentions it. A maintainer fixing that message to name 'secret' now breaks jsonObjectWithoutSecretOrEncodingNamesTheRequiredEncoding, which asserts the wrong string exactly.

text: The new equality test asserts Discriminator equality and hashing "by byte values", but DiscriminatorRecord.equals accepts any Discriminator while its hashCode does not — so equality is asymmetric and hash-inconsistent against the lambda implementations this same commit introduces, and the test pins only the safe record-to-record half.
scenario: Discriminator lambda = () -> new byte[]{1, 2, 3}; Discriminator record = Discriminator.createDiscriminator(new byte[]{1, 2, 3}); then record.equals(lambda) is true but lambda.equals(record) is false (Object identity), violating Object.equals symmetry. Practically: map.put(lambda, handler); map.get(record) returns null even though record.equals(lambda) reports them equal, because lambda.hashCode() is identity-based while record.hashCode() is Arrays.hashCode(data). Any consumer of this published interface that implements Discriminator itself — the documented and intended use, since it is a functional interface — and keys a Map or Set on it hits this.

text: The new javadoc publishes a claim about an unvalidated-input path — "the final payload is skipped without checking its end" — that no test pins; the accompanying test explicitly disclaims that half, so the sentence can silently go stale in either direction.
scenario: Truncate LEGACY_TX one byte inside its final instruction's data payload (dataLengthOffset + getByteLen + len - 1). deserializeSkeleton returns a skeleton rather than throwing, and skeleton.parseInstructions(accounts) returns an Instruction whose offset() + len() exceeds data().length; a later Discriminator.test(ix) on it throws IndexOutOfBoundsException from Objects.checkFromIndexSize far from the malformed input. Nothing in the suite observes this, so a future change that either adds an end-of-payload check or moves the cursor arithmetic makes the published javadoc false with a green build.

text: The rpc README institutionalizes a red mutation gate as a fourth outcome, which AGENTS.md forbids and which blocks the pre-release hardeningCertify for 25.11.0 - even though a legal close needing no production change and no owner decision is already fully argued three lines above.

scenario: A reviewer chasing `software.sava.rpc.json.PrivateKeyEncoding$Parser,createSigner,NakedReceiverMutator,NO_COVERAGE # line 137` opens PrivateKeyEncoding.java:137 and finds `if (secretMark == 0) {` - a line with no instance-method receiver at all, so no NakedReceiverMutator can be generated there. text: The rewritten larger-transaction-SIMD bullet claims account limits vary by transaction format, which is false in sava and in SIMD-0385, and it removes the only pointer to the single constant a syncer would actually have to change.
scenario: A maintainer performing an Agave sync after a SIMD raises the account limit follows AGAVE_SYNC.md:794-796, which tells them the built-in implementations apply per-format limits and that "account limits can also vary by format". They look for a v1 account-limit override analogous to `V1Transaction.exceedsSizeLimit`. None exists: `exceedsAccountLimit()` is a single un-overridden interface default reading the one shared `MAX_ACCOUNTS = 64`. They either conclude a per-format check is missing and add one, or miss `Transaction.MAX_ACCOUNTS` entirely — the old bullet named it explicitly, the rewrite does not name it anywhere.

text: The legacy 1232-byte limit now has no named home: it is an unnamed literal in two unrelated production bodies, and it is the only one of the interface's four limit defaults that does not reference a constant.
scenario: A maintainer implementing a limit-raising SIMD greps the tx package for the limit. Every other limit is greppable by name — `MAX_ACCOUNTS`, `BaseTransaction.MAX_INSTRUCTIONS`, `TxBuilderImpl.MAX_V1_SIGNATURES`, `TxBuilderImpl.MAX_SERIALIZED_LENGTH_V1` — but the legacy size limit can only be found by grepping the bare digits `1232`, which in this repo also matches unrelated content (`KitV1VectorTests.java:132`'s `a6f1232d...` lockfile digest, `ParseRpcResponseTests.java:593`'s `67734071498701232L`, and three RPC response fixtures). They update `TransactionRecord.java:382` and miss `Transaction.java:775`, so every third-party implementation that inherits the default — the exact audience the javadoc at :771-773 addresses — silently keeps the old limit while the built-ins move. Nothing asserts the two literals are equal; each is pinned by a separate test, so neither test flags the divergence.

text: The tx suite's "shadowed default" acceptance family documents baseline rows that no longer exist and justifies them with a rationale that is now false, and its line reference points at unrelated code that this commit shifted further out of alignment.
scenario: A maintainer triaging a future `Transaction.exceedsSizeLimit` survivor consults the reason register required by AGENTS.md, reads "the interface default is overridden by `TransactionRecord`, the only implementation — structurally unreachable", and accepts the mutant as an equivalent. That rationale is wrong on both counts: `V1Transaction` is a second overriding implementation, and the default is directly executed by `PreV1Transaction`, which by design inherits every v1-era method. A live survivor on that default would be waved through as structurally unreachable when it is in fact covered and killable. Separately, "line 652" resolves inside `Transaction.sign(Collection<Signer>, byte[], int, int, int)`, not `exceedsSizeLimit`.

text: The stated replacement for `Transaction.MAX_SERIALIZED_LENGTH` only works when the caller holds a `Transaction`; callers that measured raw bytes are left with no replacement, and the SDK now exposes the value nowhere.
scenario: A consumer had `if (serializedTx.length > Transaction.MAX_SERIALIZED_LENGTH) { ... }` over a `byte[]` — base64-decoded from a `getTransaction` response, or a payload sized for a UDP send buffer — with no `Transaction` instance in hand. Following the table row, they look for `exceedsSizeLimit()`; it is an instance method on `Transaction`, and the raw-bytes type sava offers (`TransactionSkeleton`, produced by `deserializeSkeleton`) exposes no size-limit accessor at all. There is no remaining public constant, method or field in the published API that yields 1232, so the only migration is to hard-code the number — which the table does not say. MIGRATION.md's own prose at :70-74 supplies the value, so the guidance is recoverable but the table row is not actionable on its own.

text: The EXTENSION_NAMES index is no longer bounded by the same value that gates the UnknownTokenExtension fallback, so a dispatch case added past index 28 turns a valid on-chain account into an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException escaping Token2022.read.
scenario: Pre-commit, one value (`extensionTypes.length`) both gated the Unknown fallback and bounded the array read, so the index was structurally safe, and the enum switch had no `default` arm — adding a constant to ExtensionType was a compile error until a case arm was added. Post-commit the fallback is `default ->` while EXTENSION_NAMES is an independent 29-element literal list. Concrete drift: SPL ships extension 29, a maintainer follows AGAVE_SYNC.md step 4 and adds `NewExt.ordinal() { return 29; }` plus `case 29 -> NewExt.read(data, i)` but omits the EXTENSION_NAMES entry (nothing forces it — the array is private, its length is asserted nowhere, and `check` compiles clean). Parsing any mainnet mint carrying type 29 then reaches line 117 with extensionType=29 and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 29 out of bounds for length 29` out of `Token2022.read` — an undeclared unchecked exception on a well-formed account, instead of the parsed extension. The pre-commit code could not produce this failure at all.

text: EXTENSION_NAMES[16] and [17] are provably unreachable dead entries whose real values are duplicated as string literals in the two requireLength calls, so a wrong name at those two indices is undetectable by any test.
scenario: Change EXTENSION_NAMES[16] from "ConfidentialTransferFeeConfig" to any other string and the whole suite still passes, because no execution path can print it. For extensionType 16: if `length != ConfidentialTransferFeeConfig.BYTES`, `requireLength("ConfidentialTransferFeeConfig", ...)` at line 90 throws first using its own hard-coded literal; if `length == BYTES`, `ConfidentialTransferFeeConfig.read` cannot return null (it only nulls on `data == null || data.length == 0`, impossible inside the loop) and its `l()` is `65 + (to - i - 65) == length`, so neither the `extensionData == null` message nor the `parsedLength != length` message at lines 118-131 can fire. Ordinal 17 is identical (`l() == to - offset == length`), and index 0 is unreachable because `extensionType == 0` early-returns as padding. The conformance test's new message assertion (SolanaUpstreamLayoutConformanceTests:152-159) pins the requireLength literals for rows 16 and 17, never the array entries — so 3 of the 29 rows in the table this commit introduced to 'preserve diagnostic names' carry zero coverage, and the names for two live wire IDs exist in two places that nothing keeps in sync.

text: Switching the decoder from the shared `RpcEncoding` to a private `DataEncoding` copy drops the compile-time guarantee that sava can decode every encoding it can request; a future request encoding now silently decodes to an empty byte array instead of failing the build.
scenario: Add a fourth constant to `RpcEncoding` (e.g. `base64_lz4("base64+lz4")`, or any future Solana encoding) and its `PARSER` arm, then call `ProgramAccountsRequest.build().encoding(RpcEncoding.base64_lz4)...`. The client emits `"encoding":"base64+lz4"` (ProgramAccountsRequestRecord.java:44), the node replies `["<payload>","base64+lz4"]`, `DATA_ENCODING_PARSER` falls through to `return null` (JsonUtil.java:39), and `case null -> new byte[0]` (JsonUtil.java:78) hands every `AccountInfo.data()` an empty array — no exception, and unlike the non-array fallback at line 85 not even a WARNING log. Before this commit the identical change did not compile: `switch (encoding)` at old line 58 was an exhaustive enum switch expression over `RpcEncoding` with no `default`, so adding a constant produced a compile error in JsonUtil that forced the decoder to be updated in lockstep.

text: The commit states the `NakedReceiverMutator` on `ji.reset(mark2).skipRestOfArray()` is now killed, yet keeps its `SURVIVED` acceptance row, so `pitestResponsesVerify` can no longer detect that mutant re-surviving.
scenario: A later refactor makes the unknown-encoding arm consume the data element (e.g. `case null -> { ji.skip(); yield new byte[0]; }`), which restores position-equivalence for the reset-drop and makes the NakedReceiver mutant survive again. `pitestResponsesVerify` diffs the run's unkilled mutants against the line-less key `JsonUtil,parseEncodedData,NakedReceiverMutator,SURVIVED`, finds it already accepted, and passes — the assertion power this commit just bought is lost with no signal.

text: Three of the six `JsonUtil` baseline rows kept `# line` tags from a much older tree; after this commit's 17-line insertion they resolve into the newly added `DataEncoding` block, so the documented anchors point at unrelated code.
scenario: A maintainer triaging the live `# single element array` acceptance (argued at README.md:335-341) follows the authoritative anchor to JsonUtil.java:28 and lands on an enum constant list with no conditional and no return — the mutant it argues about is 40 lines further down. The same happens for `JsonUtil.parseEncodedData:37` in the README heading, which now names `return DataEncoding.base58;`.

text: The EXTENSION_NAMES lookup is no longer structurally bounded - the old code proved its array index in range with an explicit length guard, while the new code relies on an unenforced convention that every non-default case label is < EXTENSION_NAMES.length.
scenario: SPL ships extension type 29 and a maintainer follows AGAVE_SYNC.md step 4 but appends only the record, its `ordinal()` and `case 29 -> NewExt.read(data, i)`, forgetting the 30th EXTENSION_NAMES entry. Every account carrying a type-29 TLV whose declared length disagrees with the parsed length (or a zero-length one) then makes `parseExtensions` throw `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 29 out of bounds for length 29` from line 117 instead of the `IllegalArgumentException` that AGAVE_SYNC.md and the conformance fixture document - an unchecked crash out of a public parser on ordinary malformed on-chain data. The pre-commit code could not fail this way: `extensionTypes[extensionType]` at old line 48 was reachable only after `if (extensionType >= extensionTypes.length) { ...; continue; }` at old line 41, so the index was provably valid for all 65,536 inputs.

text: The commit removed the only assertion tying the Java extension-type population to the pinned Rust fixture at the same time as the compiler stopped enforcing dispatch exhaustiveness, so a known extension can now be added to the sealed hierarchy with no dispatch arm and `./gradlew check` stays green.
scenario: A maintainer adds `PermissionedTransfer` to `MintTokenExtension`'s permits clause with `ordinal() { return 29; }`, `l()` and `write()`, but omits `case 29 ->` in parseExtensions. `TokenExtension.write` happily emits a type-29 TLV, but `Token2022.parseExtensions` returns `UnknownTokenExtension(29, raw)` for it, so `parseExtensions(write(x))` no longer round-trips to `x` - and no test fails, because the sealed hierarchy's size is asserted nowhere and the fixture still has 29 rows. Before this commit the same omission was a compile error twice over: `extensionType()` was abstract so the record needed an `ExtensionType` constant, that constant made the `switch (type)` over the enum non-exhaustive, and `assertEquals(javaTypes.length, fixture.rows().size())` failed against the 29-row fixture.

text: parseAccountType still clones the AccountType enum's backing array on every account parse, the same per-call `values()` allocation this commit just eliminated from parseExtensions.
scenario: Reading a page of N Token-2022 mints or token accounts (e.g. a getProgramAccounts sweep) allocates N throwaway three-element `AccountType[]` arrays - `Enum.values()` defensively clones on each invocation - purely to bounds-check one byte. Parsing 10,000 accounts is 10,000 needless array allocations on the hot decode path.

text: MIGRATION.md's title and the README link name "the v1 release", a library version that cannot exist and that collides with this repo's established meaning of "v1" (the v1 transaction format).
scenario: A consumer on 25.10.0 hits a compile error after upgrading, opens README.md, and reads "Upcoming v1 release migration". They conclude the removals ship in a future release that also brings v1 transactions, and defer migrating. In fact the very next release carries them: .release-please-manifest.json is `{".": "25.10.0"}` and release-please-config.json sets `"versioning": "always-bump-patch"`, so this commit produces 25.10.1. No release named "v1" is reachable even by a manual `chore: release X` override, because 1.0.0 sorts BELOW the published 25.10.0 in both Gradle and Maven ordering, so it could never be published as an upgrade. Worse, MIGRATION.md uses "v1" in its own repo-standard sense four lines later -- line 5-6 "their removal is deferred until v1 is activated on mainnet" and line 72 "4,096 bytes for v1" -- so the title and the body mean two different things by the same token. `grep -rn "v1 release"` over the repo returns only these two lines; every other "v1" in AGAVE_SYNC.md, Transaction.java and TxBuilderImpl.java means the transaction format.

text: The RPC section frames the parseEncoding change as benign and offers no replacement, but sava's own response parser used RpcEncoding.parseEncoding for responses and its successor, JsonUtil.DataEncoding, is private -- leaving consumers with a compile-clean silent break and nowhere to go.
scenario: Before this commit, JsonUtil itself parsed a *response's* encoding field with `RpcEncoding.parseEncoding(ji)` (0112d69^:JsonUtil.java:55) and switched on `case base58 ->`, and RpcEncoding's own class doc called it "Wire encodings for account and transaction data" -- not request-only. A consumer who mirrored that pattern in a hand-written jsoniter parser (`switch (RpcEncoding.parseEncoding(ji)) { case base58 -> ...; case base64 -> ...; }`) now compiles unchanged, because base64/base64_zstd still exist. At runtime, an `"encoding": "base58"` element in a getAccountInfo response makes parseEncoding return null: a classic `switch` on the null throws NullPointerException, and an enhanced switch without `case null` throws MatchException. MIGRATION.md's table has no row for this, and its prose calls base58 one of the "other unsupported request names" -- but base58 is a fully supported *response* name that JsonUtil still decodes (JsonUtil.java:75). The only remaining encoding parser that recognises it, `DataEncoding` / `DATA_ENCODING_PARSER`, is `private` (JsonUtil.java:27, :31), so no public replacement is offered anywhere. The commit message's "Preserve ... incoming base58 response decoding" is therefore only half true: sava's internal decoder preserves it, the public parser consumers were pointed at does not.

text: MIGRATION.md says the legacy/v0 factories' *removal* is deferred until v1 activates on mainnet, but every TODO in the code says activation triggers their *deprecation*, not their removal.
scenario: Per the repo's own notes, `enable_tx_v1` is already active on testnet and devnet and only mainnet remains. A consumer reading MIGRATION.md line 5-6 plans a migration off `Transaction.createTx(...)` for the release immediately following mainnet activation, because the guide told them removal lands there. The code's plan is the opposite: 23 `// TODO: deprecate once v1 transactions are active on mainnet` blocks in Transaction.java and 7 more in TransactionSkeleton.java say activation only turns the deprecation annotations on, with removal some unspecified releases later. The reader either front-loads work that isn't due, or -- reading the guide as authoritative -- is surprised when the activation release compiles fine but emits deprecation warnings it never mentioned.

text: The rewrite deleted the ordinal append-order rule while the replacement design introduced a positionally indexed EXTENSION_NAMES array, and neither the Token-2022 section nor sync step 4 states that the array must stay dense and index-aligned from 0.
scenario: Sync step 4 now reads "add the record to the sealed `TokenExtension` hierarchy, its fixed `ordinal()`, dispatch case and diagnostic name" -- it names the diagnostic name but never says the names table is indexed by raw wire ID, nor even names `EXTENSION_NAMES`. The removed text carried exactly that ordering rule ("new SPL extensions are appended, so new Java entries must be appended in the same order"). `Token2022.parseExtensions` indexes `EXTENSION_NAMES[extensionType]` unconditionally for any type that fell through to a dispatch case (Token2022.java:117). So a syncer who supports a new SPL extension out of order -- e.g. upstream reserves ID 29 for a test-only or unsupportable variant and ships ID 30, so the syncer adds `case 30 ->` and appends "NewExt" as the 30th element (index 29) -- makes every parse of a real mainnet account carrying that extension throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from `EXTENSION_NAMES[30]`, before any of the length checks below it run. Under the pre-commit design the enum constant carried its own `name()`, so this failure mode did not exist and the deleted rule was the only thing guarding the new one.
